standard_prerequisites.name: Scale-invariant spacing process
standard_prerequisites.statement: The points S_i indexed by the integers form a Poisson process on the positive half-line with intensity ds/s.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the process transformed in the proof.

standard_prerequisites.name: Mapping theorem for Poisson processes
standard_prerequisites.statement: A measurable image of a Poisson process is again a Poisson process with the pushed-forward mean measure, provided that measure has no atoms.
standard_prerequisites.use: It transports the process to the real line.

standard_prerequisites.name: GEM distribution
standard_prerequisites.statement: The GEM distribution is the law of the decreasing rearrangement of the atoms obtained by cutting a unit interval at independent geometric proportions.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the law asserted for the normalised gaps.

core_obligations: Apply the increasing map sending s to log base 2 of x minus log s to the points of the spacing process, so that the mapping theorem gives a homogeneous Poisson process of rate one on the real line (source line 712).

Read off the decreasing gaps between consecutive points of that homogeneous process as the successive differences of an ordered sample, which are the geometric proportions defining the GEM distribution (source line 712).
Conclude that the normalised vector displayed in the statement follows the GEM distribution (source line 712).

proof_roadmap.step: Transport the scale-invariant process to a homogeneous process of rate one on the real line.
Identify the normalised gaps with the proportions of a GEM partition.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled proposition at source lines 706-709: the vector formed by one minus the first gap and the successive later gaps, all divided by the logarithm of x, follows a GEM distribution. The proof (source lines 711-713) is a single change of variables, but the step is not formal: the scale-invariant spacing process has to be transported by the map sending s to the base-two logarithm of x minus the logarithm of s, the mapping theorem has to be invoked to know that the image is again a Poisson process, now homogeneous of rate one on the whole real line, and the ordered points of that process have to be recognised as producing the geometric proportions that define the GEM distribution. The statement records only the resulting law.
